title: A Night Without Explanations
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The dinner was soup, slightly burnt bread, and a very poor argument about punctuation.

Severus was winning.

He had found a note I'd written for the Moonroot records cabinet. I had put a comma in a place he considered offensive. He had circled it twice and written "WHY?" in the margin.

"I thought we were having a quiet evening," I said.

"We are."

"Then why is my comma on trial?"

"Because it committed a crime."

I stared at him.

He looked perfectly serious.

It was one of the reasons I loved him.

We'd planned the evening two weeks earlier. No archive work after six. No visitors unless the house was on fire. No promises that every difficult feeling had to be discussed before we could have dinner. Severus had chosen the soup. I had bought the bread. Both of us had underestimated how quickly bread could burn when we became distracted by an argument about semicolons.

He cut away the darkest edge.

"There," he said. "Salvaged."

"You sound like Tamsin."

"An alarming comparison."

I poured the soup.

It wasn't elegant. The table was too small for the good dishes, the room was chilly, and the rain had begun tapping against the windows. The ordinary life of Spinner's End pressed close around us.

For once, we let it.

After dinner, Severus took a book from the shelf and sat in the chair by the lamp. I settled on the sofa with my green notebook. The pages still held the list I'd written after finding my old room: things I wanted, things I was afraid to ask for, small choices that belonged to me.

I wrote one sentence.

I want tonight to remain ordinary.

Severus looked up.

"What are you writing?"

"A sentence."

"That explains very little."

"I know."

He raised an eyebrow.

I smiled and closed the notebook.

He returned to his book.

The quiet was not empty. It had the sounds of a house occupied by people who didn't have to entertain each other: paper turning, the occasional creak of the old floor, rainwater in the gutter, the kettle beginning to cool.

After an hour, Severus shut his book.

"Are you comfortable?" he asked.

"Yes."

"Would you prefer the fire higher?"

"I'm fine."

He studied me.

"That wasn't an invitation to endure the cold out of politeness."

I laughed.

"All right. A little higher would be nice."

He adjusted the fire with a small spell, then returned to the chair.

I watched him.

"What?" he asked.

"Nothing."

"Jasper."

"I like seeing you relaxed."

He looked almost offended.

"I am not relaxed."

"Your shoulders have dropped."

"They are merely tired."

"Your book is on the wrong shelf."

His eyes widened.

I laughed before he could find a defense.

He stood, crossed the room, and took the book from my hands.

"You are becoming intolerable."

"I've had a good teacher."

He put the book aside.

Then he sat beside me.

The sofa was narrow. Our knees touched. I could feel the warmth of him through the fabric of his trousers, and the scent of old paper and tea clung to his sleeves.

"May I?" he asked, lifting a hand toward my face.

I nodded.

His fingers brushed a strand of hair from my cheek. The gesture was so careful that my chest tightened.

"You don't have to ask every time," I whispered.

"I know."

"Then why do you?"

"Because I enjoy hearing you choose."

I leaned toward him.

"Yes."

He kissed me slowly, then drew back just far enough to see my face. There was no urgency. No need to prove we'd survived another difficult conversation. We'd made time, kept it, and arrived at this moment on purpose.

I kissed him again.

When the rain grew heavier, he asked whether I wanted to stay.

"I do."

We left the books where they were, turned down the lamps, and closed the bedroom door. The rest of the evening remained ours.

In the morning, the kettle was empty and the bread was still terrible.

Severus made tea.

I made porridge.

He glanced at the calendar pinned beside the kitchen door.

"Moonroot at ten," he said.

"I know."

"Neri wishes to review the revised catalog access forms."

"I know."

"Orin is due at eleven."

"Severus."

He looked at me.

"Yes?"

"I can read."

His mouth twitched.

"An ability I have never questioned."

I kissed his cheek and reached for the porridge.

We arrived at the archive on time. Neri had the new forms ready, with separate spaces for public engineering records and private correspondence. Orin arrived carrying a revised essay that no longer began by calling Severus a saint.

The work was difficult and ordinary.

At noon, I found the note with the criminal comma on the table.

Severus had corrected it again.

This time he'd added a small line beneath the margin.

I LIKE YOUR SENTENCES EVEN WHEN THEY ARE WRONG.

I looked toward his desk.

He refused to look up.

I wrote underneath:

AND I LIKE YOUR BOOKS EVEN WHEN YOU PUT THEM IN THE WRONG ORDER.

He made a disapproving sound.

It was a very good morning.
